title: Left Hand Limit
notes: **Definition.** lim(x→a⁻) f(x) = L means f(x) → L as x approaches a from the left through values x < a; it is written LHL or f(a − 0).
**Substitution trick.** Put x = a − h with h > 0 and h → 0, so lim(x→a⁻) f(x) = lim(h→0⁺) f(a − h).
**Worked example.** lim(x→0⁻) |x|/x = lim(x→0⁻) (−x)/x = −1, because |x| = −x for negative x; combined with RHL = 1 this proves lim(x→0) |x|/x does not exist.
**Piecewise functions.** For a rule that changes at a, use the branch valid for x < a when computing the LHL, and the other branch for the RHL.
**Radicals and logs.** lim(x→0⁺) √x = 0 has a right-hand limit but no left-hand limit, because √x and ln x are undefined for x < 0 in the reals.
**Exam caution.** A two-sided limit cannot be inferred from the LHL alone; always compute both one-sided limits before concluding existence.
summary: The left-hand limit approaches a through values smaller than a; x = a − h with h → 0⁺ is the standard evaluation method.
